segments.text: A social problem is a condition that causes significant harm, affects many people or social institutions, and becomes a matter of public concern requiring collective response. The syllabus lists a wide range of problems in Pakistan.
Do not prepare this chapter as isolated definitions. Use one common framework for every issue: meaning → causes → consequences → affected groups → institutions involved → practical responses.

items.text: Population growth and migration

: Rapid population growth and rural–urban migration can place pressure on jobs, housing, schools, health services and infrastructure, but outcomes depend on planning, productivity and service capacity.
Technical and vocational training
: A mismatch between education, skills and labour-market needs can reduce employability and productivity. Training quality, access, industry linkages and certification matter.
Deviance and street crime

: Deviance means violation of social norms; crime means violation of law. Street crime should be explained through multiple factors such as opportunity, inequality, peer networks, policing, drugs and local conditions rather than one cause.
Unemployment

: Unemployment has economic and social consequences for households, identity, marriage decisions, migration and social trust. Causes can include slow job creation, skills mismatch, economic cycles and structural change.
Illiteracy and school dropout

: Education problems can reflect poverty, distance, school quality, household labour needs, gender barriers, disability, language and opportunity costs. Responses need both access and learning quality.
Smuggling
: Smuggling involves illegal movement of goods or persons across legal controls. It can be encouraged by price differentials, weak enforcement, corruption, difficult borders and organized networks.
Prostitution

: Treat this topic with non-stigmatizing language. Analysis may consider poverty, coercion, trafficking, gender inequality, demand, law, health and exploitation while distinguishing consensual adult sex work from trafficking and abuse.
Poverty
: Poverty is multidimensional: low income interacts with poor health, weak education, insecure work, housing and limited opportunity. Structural and household-level factors should both be examined.
Drug addiction

: Substance-use disorders involve biological, psychological and social factors. Prevention, treatment, harm reduction where legally/medically appropriate, family support and law enforcement address different parts of the problem.
Child labour and abuse

: Child labour can interfere with education, health and development; abuse includes physical, emotional and sexual harm and neglect. Poverty, weak protection systems and harmful norms can increase vulnerability.
Bonded labour
: Bonded labour involves coercive labour linked with debt or dependency and raises serious legal and human-rights concerns. Study economic vulnerability, enforcement and labour relations.
Customs affecting women; violence and domestic violence
: Analyse discriminatory practices through power, law, economic dependency, social norms, access to justice and support services. Avoid victim-blaming.
Issues concerning the elderly

: Older people may face income insecurity, health needs, caregiving gaps, loneliness, age discrimination and weak social protection. Family change and migration can alter traditional support arrangements.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

blocks.text: How to analyze a social problem

segments.text: A social problem is not simply any condition someone dislikes. It is a condition widely recognized as harmful, affecting significant groups and connected to social structures or institutions. Good analysis separates description from explanation and avoids blaming affected people for conditions produced by interacting economic, institutional and cultural factors.

items.text: Scale
: Use a reliable indicator to establish how widespread or severe the issue is. State the source and year.
Causes
: Separate structural causes such as labour markets or unequal services from institutional, community, household and individual-level factors.
Consequences
: Trace effects on health, education, family, economy, security and social trust without assuming every affected person experiences all outcomes.
Responses
: Distinguish prevention, protection, service delivery, enforcement and long-term structural reform.

segments.text: Pakistan's 2023 census recorded 241.49 million people and an intercensal average annual growth rate of 2.55 percent for 2017-2023. Population growth matters because it raises the scale at which schools, housing, jobs, water and health services must expand. It should not be used as a one-cause explanation for every social problem; service capacity, productivity, governance and spatial distribution matter equally.

PBS HIES 2024-25 reports a total fertility rate of 3.6 children per woman. Fertility is related to child survival, education, family preferences, reproductive health access and economic conditions. Policy should therefore focus on informed choice and services rather than coercive assumptions.

PBS HIES 2024-25 reports a literacy rate of 63 percent for the population aged 10 years and older and an out-of-school rate of 28 percent among children aged 5-16. These are national indicators and should not be treated as identical across provinces, gender or income groups.

items.text: Access
: Distance, cost, household income, safety and availability of schools affect enrollment.
Quality
: Enrollment does not guarantee learning. Teacher capacity, attendance, curriculum, language and school management shape outcomes.
Inequality
: Gender, disability, region and household wealth can create unequal pathways. Targeted support must therefore complement general expansion.
Labour-market connection
: Education policy should build foundational learning and relevant skills without reducing education to job training alone.

segments.text: PBS reports an unemployment rate of 7.1 percent in the Labour Force Survey 2024-25 and labour-force participation of 46.3 percent. Unemployment is only one labour-market problem: underemployment, low productivity, informality, skills mismatch and low female participation also affect economic security.

items.text: Demand side
: Slow job creation, sectoral change and investment conditions determine how many positions exist.
Supply side
: Education and skills affect employability, but training alone cannot solve unemployment when aggregate demand for labour is weak.
Institutions
: Labour regulation, transport, childcare, discrimination and information networks influence who can access work.

segments.text: Poverty is multidimensional: low income interacts with poor housing, weak health access, educational exclusion, insecure work and vulnerability to shocks. Monetary poverty lines are essential for measurement but do not capture every deprivation.

items.text: Intergenerational transmission
: Poor nutrition, weak schooling and limited networks can reduce later opportunities, making poverty persistent across generations.
Shocks
: Illness, inflation, disaster or job loss can push vulnerable households into poverty even when they were previously above a poverty line.
Social protection
: Cash transfers, insurance, food or nutrition support and public services can reduce immediate harm, while employment, education and health systems address longer-term capability.
Crime

: Crime rates are shaped by opportunity, policing, inequality, social networks, age structure, markets and reporting practices. Rising recorded crime can reflect more offending, better reporting or both.
Substance-use problems
: Drug use should be analyzed through availability, dependence, mental health, family context and organized markets. Stigma can discourage treatment.
Violence

: Interpersonal and collective violence have different causes and should not be collapsed into a single explanation. Prevention may require justice reform, youth opportunity, community intervention and control of illicit markets.

blocks.text: Gender inequality and violence against women

segments.text: Gender inequality operates through education, labour markets, property, unpaid care work, representation and safety. An analytical answer distinguishes legal equality from actual access and implementation.

items.text: Violence
: Gender-based violence is sustained by power imbalance, harmful norms, impunity and service gaps. Avoid victim-blaming; responsibility lies with perpetrators and enabling institutions.
Economic participation
: Transport, workplace safety, childcare, social norms and occupational segregation affect women's employment in addition to education.
Policy
: Effective responses combine law, enforcement, survivor-centred services, prevention, economic opportunity and public accountability.

blocks.text: Child labour, youth and the elderly

items.text: Child labour

: Poverty, adult unemployment, school access, household shocks and demand for cheap labour contribute. Not every form of children's work is legally or sociologically equivalent, so analysis should distinguish hazardous or exploitative labour from age-appropriate household contribution.
Youth

: A large young population can expand the labour force and innovation if education, health and jobs grow sufficiently. Without opportunity, prolonged unemployment and exclusion can intensify frustration and migration pressure.
Elderly

: Population ageing increases needs for income security, chronic-disease care and caregiving. Family support remains important but migration and smaller households can weaken traditional arrangements, increasing the importance of social protection and accessible services.

segments.text: Rapid city growth increases demand for land, transport, water, drainage, waste management and housing. Problems emerge when planning and municipal finance fail to keep pace. Informal settlement should therefore be treated as a land-and-governance issue as well as a poverty issue.

Environmental hazards such as heat, air pollution and flooding affect social groups unequally because exposure and housing quality differ. Sociology adds the distributional question: who is most exposed, who has resources to adapt and whose neighbourhood receives protective infrastructure?
Reading the flow: each step creates the conditions for the next; the arrows show sequence or influence, not inevitability unless the text explicitly says so.

items.text: Use the same 6-part framework for every social problem.
Add statistics only after checking the latest official source and date.
Always distinguish correlation from causation and avoid blaming affected groups.
Prepare 3–4 strong problems in depth and the rest in concise frameworks, then update evidence before the exam.

rows: Avoid this error Do not fill answers with random statistics from coaching material. A small number of recent, official, correctly dated figures is far better than many uncertain numbers.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define the social problem, identify causes at multiple levels, explain consequences, identify affected groups/institutions, then propose realistic preventive and corrective responses.
• Conerly, Holmes, & Tamang, Introduction to Sociology 3e (OpenStax, 2021).
• Pakistan Bureau of Statistics: Population and Housing Census 2023; Labour Force Survey 2024-25; HIES 2024-25 indicators available on PBS in 2026.
• Most social problems have interacting structural, institutional, community and individual causes.
• Problems often reinforce one another—for example poverty, dropout, unemployment and crime risk.
• Law alone is rarely enough; prevention, services, education and economic policy also matter.
• Use respectful, non-stigmatizing language.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
